analysis.one_liner: Requires private insurers to cover COVID-19 tests at no out-of-pocket cost during the declared emergency.
analysis.headline: The bill was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced and never received a vote before the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: During the COVID-19 public health emergency, the bill would require group health plans and private insurance to cover government-designated COVID-19 tests with no copays, deductibles, or other cost sharing. It would also require the federal vaccine advisory committee to issue a recommendation on any FDA-licensed COVID-19 vaccine within 15 business days. The bill was introduced on March 12, 2020 by Rep. Larry Bucshon (R-IN) with Rep. Jan Schakowsky (D-IL) as its sole cosponsor, and was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: People with private insurance who needed a COVID-19 test: they could get government-designated tests without paying anything out of pocket, and a licensed COVID-19 vaccine would get a formal federal coverage recommendation within about three weeks of approval.

how_it_helps.text: Private health plans and insurers must cover Secretary-designated COVID-19 testing services with no cost sharing for the duration of the January 31, 2020 public health emergency declaration [S2][S3].

The Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices must meet and issue a recommendation on a licensed COVID-19 vaccine within 15 business days of FDA licensure, instead of the longer timeline under the 21st Century Cures Act [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and the employers and policyholders who fund group plans bear the cost of free testing, likely passed through premiums; in exchange, testing labs gain a guaranteed paying customer base.

drawbacks.text: The mandate's cost falls on insurers and employers, and those costs are typically passed to workers and policyholders through higher premiums [S3].

The coverage mandate is narrow and temporary: it applies only to tests the Secretary specifies and only during the declared emergency, ending when the declaration terminates or when the US Preventive Services Task Force rates the test [S3].

A good-faith objection to the vaccine provision: forcing the advisory committee to issue a recommendation within 15 business days of licensure could compress the evidence review that normally guards against a rushed or premature vaccine recommendation [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For insured people during a pandemic, free testing was a clear and affordable benefit: the emergency scope and Secretary designation kept the mandate limited, and the premium cost of covering cheap diagnostics was small compared with the public-health value of widespread testing. The 15-business-day vaccine deadline is the weakest part of the bill, since it prioritizes speed over deliberation, though it applies only to vaccines already FDA-licensed.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Larry Bucshon (R-IN) introduced the bill on March 12, 2020, with Rep. Jan Schakowsky (D-IL) as its one cosponsor [S1][S4].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on March 12, 2020; the action history shows no further steps — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote [S5].
The 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 without the bill ever advancing, so it expired [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Insured patients lost little in practice, because Congress enacted no-cost COVID-19 testing requirements in relief legislation just days later in March 2020; the insurers and employers who would have funded the mandate under this bill avoided it only for about a week, and the committee leadership that never acted on it faced no consequence for the gap.

for.name: Rep. Larry Bucshon
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee, where he sits.

against.name: Rep. Frank Pallone
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee hearing, markup, or vote; it sat without action until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by a Republican and cosponsored by a Democrat, but it died in committee with no recorded floor votes, so no partisan voting pattern exists.

industries.note: The bill forces insurers to cover designated COVID-19 tests with no cost sharing, bearing that cost themselves and through premiums. Insurers benefit from an insured population that tests more, but the mandate's immediate effect is a new required expense during an emergency.

Guaranteed coverage without cost sharing removes the price barrier that keeps patients from getting tested, sending more paying customers to labs. More testing also serves the public goal of controlling the outbreak.
Group plans would have to fund free testing for employees and dependents, a cost employers typically pass back through plan contributions or premiums.
